title: Why Doesn't a Helicopter Spin Out of Control?
description:
Start the engine of a normal helicopter, take away one small part at the back, and the whole machine would spin around in circles the moment it tried to lift off. That small part is the tail rotor, and it is only the beginning. Helicopters are full of parts that look strange from the ground, a fan inside the tail, a nut with a nickname, blades that cut cables. Today, ten parts that keep a helicopter from spinning, shaking or falling, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:17 1. The tail rotor
2:47 2. The fan inside the tail
4:21 3. The tail with no rotor
5:53 4. The two rotors on top
7:18 5. The rotor at each end
8:38 6. The plates under the rotor
10:01 7. The nut on top
11:22 8. The dampers on the blades
12:47 9. The blades above the cockpit
14:12 10. The clutch that lets go
15:45 The verdict

Sources:
- Tail rotor, about 10% of engine power, Sikorsky layout, stripes for ground crew visibility: Wikipedia, "Tail rotor" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tail_rotor
- Fenestron first flight 12 April 1968 (Gazelle prototype), uneven blade spacing on H135, H160 canted 12 degrees: Airbus, "50th anniversary of the trademark Fenestron" https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2018-04-50th-anniversary-of-the-trademark-fenestron
- NOTAR (Coanda slots, direct jet thruster, OH-6A first flight 17 Dec 1981, 520N 1990, among the quietest FAA-certified): Wikipedia, "NOTAR" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOTAR
- Coaxial rotors (Kamov, torque cancellation): Wikipedia, "Coaxial-rotor aircraft" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaxial-rotor_aircraft
- CH-47 Chinook tandem rotors, first flight September 1961: Wikipedia, "Boeing CH-47 Chinook" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_CH-47_Chinook
- Swashplate, collective and cyclic: FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/helicopter_flying_handbook.pdf
- Jesus nut (1967 print, Bell 206B crash in 2000): Wikipedia, "Jesus nut" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_nut
- Ground resonance, lag dampers, tests, lift-off escape: SlashGear https://www.slashgear.com/1891320/ground-resonance-dangerous-to-helicopters
- Wire strike protection system (Bristol Aerospace, May 1979 Kiowa, 3/8 in cable, 16% of US Army fatalities 1974-79): Wikipedia, "Wire strike protection system" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_strike_protection_system
- Autorotation, freewheeling unit, flare at 50-100 ft, Jean Boulet Lama record 21 June 1972: Wikipedia, "Autorotation" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autorotation
